london_great_smog_1952.text: At noon on December 5, 1952, London streets darkened under dense smog for five days (Dec 5–9, 1952).
london_great_smog_1952.source: UK Met Office Great Smog 1952 archive

london_great_smog_1952.text: Coal fireplaces and coal power plants released soot and sulfur emissions into cold winter air.
A warm temperature inversion trapped cold dirty air below.
london_great_smog_1952.source: UK Met Office temperature inversion explanation

london_great_smog_1952.text: Near-zero street visibility required walkers with lanterns to guide buses.
Estimated ~4,000 excess deaths attributed to the smog event.
london_great_smog_1952.source: London City Hall / historical public health estimates

london_great_smog_1952.text: Parliament passed the Clean Air Act of 1956 promoting smokeless heating.

mount_st_helens_1980.text: At 8:32 a.m. on May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens' north flank had bulged outward by hundreds of feet above an intruding magma cryptodome.
mount_st_helens_1980.source: USGS FS 036-00 & National Volcanic Monument Geology

mount_st_helens_1980.text: A magnitude 5.1 earthquake shook loose the north flank, triggering the largest recorded subaerial landslide.
Sudden decompression of the cryptodome unleashed a lateral blast of steam, gas, and pulverized rock exceeding 300 mph.
The lateral blast flattened forests across roughly 230–250 square miles north of the crater.
Following the lateral blast, a towering vertical ash column erupted skyward for ~9 hours across downwind states.
mount_st_helens_1980.source: USGS Volcanic Ash Mount St. Helens 1980

mount_st_helens_1980.text: The collapse left a north-facing horseshoe crater and reshaped hazards monitoring of lateral volcanic blasts.
